artworks.title: The Eurytos Krater (Heracles in the House of Eurytus)
artworks.description: This Late Corinthian black-figure column-krater, now in the Louvre (E635), is the earliest surviving image to name Iole. The frieze shows the banquet of King Eurytus of Oechalia, where Heracles reclines among the king and his sons after the archery contest; the inscribed female figure Iole stands at the right of the scene, the bride who was offered as the prize and then withheld. The vase fixes in painted clay the moment that sets the whole tragedy of Heracles' death in motion, and is a key early witness to the myth tradition recorded later by Apollodorus.

artworks.title: Hercules and Iole
artworks.description: Painted for the Studiolo of Francesco I de' Medici in the Palazzo Vecchio, Florence, this Mannerist panel by Santi di Tito depicts the captive Iole brought before Heracles. Set within the prince's celebrated cabinet of curiosities, the work renders the heroine of Oechalia in the elegant, elongated grace typical of late Florentine Mannerism, treating her as the fatal prize whose presence in Heracles' household would provoke Deianira's jealousy and the hero's ruin.

artworks.title: Heracles Abducting Iole
artworks.description: This Roman marble relief in the Archaeological Museum of Piraeus shows Heracles carrying off Iole after the sack of Oechalia. Identifiable by his club and lion-skin, the hero seizes the daughter of Eurytus as his captive, the spoils of the war he waged to punish the king who had cheated him of his archery prize. The relief crystallizes the abduction that, through Deianira's fear of a rival, would lead to the poisoned robe of Nessus and the hero's death on Mount Oeta.

artworks.title: Hercules and Iole (woodcut)
artworks.description: A Renaissance book woodcut, preserved through the Penn Provenance Project, illustrating Hercules and Iole. Drawing on the late tradition that paired her with Omphale's emasculating power over the hero, the print shows Hercules clothed at once as man and as woman beside Iole, a moralizing emblem of love's power to unman even the strongest of heroes. It exemplifies how the figure of Iole survived into early printed mythography as a cautionary image.
